name: Gongura Pachadi
subtitle: fierce sour-leaf chutney, eaten by the spoonful with hot rice

ingredients.note: standing in for gongura (sorrel), which is not in the catalogue; amaranth has the same soft body but none of the sourness, so the tamarind below is doing that job
not optional here — it replaces the acidity real gongura would bring
Guntur chillies if you have them
Indian toasted gingelly oil, not the East Asian kind
a quarter teaspoon and no more
use compounded-free hing to keep this gluten-free

prepNotes: Soak the tamarind in 100ml of hot water for 20 minutes, then squeeze it to a thick pulp and discard the fibres.
Wash the greens and spread them on a cloth until bone dry — wet leaves steam instead of frying and the chutney turns watery.
Have a clean, completely dry glass jar ready; any moisture and this will not keep.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp of the sesame oil in a kadhai and fry the dried red chillies, fenugreek seeds and half the cumin over low heat for 2 minutes, until the chillies darken by a shade and smell toasty.
steps.tip: Fenugreek burns from tan to black in about ten seconds. Pull the pan off the moment it colours.

steps.text: Lift the spices out onto a plate and set them aside to cool completely.
In the same pan add another 2 tbsp oil and the garlic, and fry 2 minutes until the cloves are pale gold at the edges.
Add the greens a large handful at a time with the green chillies and turmeric, and cook over medium-high heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the leaves collapse and the pan goes almost dry.
steps.tip: Keep cooking past the point where they look done. Any water left behind will spoil the chutney within days.

steps.text: Stir in the tamarind pulp and salt and cook another 4 minutes, until the mixture pulls away from the sides of the pan in a single mass.
Cool the greens fully, then grind them with the toasted spices to a coarse paste — no water at all, and it should still have some texture.
steps.tip: Grind in short pulses. A smooth purée loses the rustic bite this is meant to have.

steps.text: Heat the last tbsp of oil, crackle the mustard seeds and remaining cumin, add the curry leaves and asafoetida, and pour the whole tempering over the chutney.
steps.tip: Wait for the mustard to actually pop before the curry leaves go in, or the tadka tastes raw.

steps.text: Fold the tempering through and taste for salt and sourness — it should hit sour first, then heat.

storage: Packed into a dry jar with a thin film of oil on top, it keeps 3 weeks refrigerated and about 5 days at room temperature. Always use a dry spoon. Serve at room temperature with hot rice and a spoon of oil.
